questions.stem: Which functional group do all alcohols contain?

options.text: The hydroxyl group, -OH
options.explanation: The -OH arrangement is what every member of the alcohol family carries.

options.text: The C=C double bond
options.explanation: That defines the alkenes; alcohols are saturated apart from the OH group.

options.text: A carboxylic acid group
options.explanation: That stronger oxidation group belongs to a different family beyond this note.

options.text: A carbon-halogen bond
options.explanation: Halogen bonds belong to the halogenoalkanes, not the alcohols.

questions.stem: What is observed when an alcohol dissolves in water?

options.text: It forms a neutral solution
options.explanation: The note states alcohols dissolve in water to form neutral solutions.

options.text: It forms an acidic solution
options.explanation: Acidity belongs to the carboxylic acids, not the alcohols here.

options.text: It forms an alkaline solution
options.explanation: The hydroxyl group is covalently bonded, not ionic like alkali hydroxides.

options.text: It will not dissolve at all
options.explanation: Dissolving is exactly what the note records them doing.

questions.stem: Why is the -OH group called the functional group of ethanol?

options.text: Because it is the part responsible for ethanol's characteristic reactions
options.explanation: The functional group is by definition the reactive arrangement steering the family chemistry.

options.text: Because it functions as the fuel itself
options.explanation: The whole molecule burns; the group name refers to reactive role, not fuel duty.

options.text: Because it adds the most mass to the molecule
options.explanation: Mass share is irrelevant to the functional group concept.

options.text: Because it was the first part discovered
options.explanation: Discovery order plays no part in the definition.

questions.stem: Why are the first four alcohols commonly used?

options.text: As fuels, because they burn releasing energy
options.explanation: The note lists the first four alcohols as commonly used fuels.

options.text: As bleaches for fabrics
options.explanation: Bleaching is not among the listed uses.

options.text: As oxidising agents in engines
options.explanation: They are the burned substance, not the supplier of oxygen.

options.text: As indicators for acidity
options.explanation: They form neutral solutions, the opposite of indicator material.

questions.stem: How do alcohols differ structurally from the alkanes they resemble?

options.text: One hydrogen is replaced by the hydroxyl group, -OH
options.explanation: The OH side chain replaces a hydrogen on the carbon chain, creating the new family.

options.text: Alcohols have a carbon-carbon double bond
options.explanation: That would make them alkenes; alcohol chains stay single-bonded.

options.text: Alcohols contain a metal atom
options.explanation: No metal appears in these molecular alcohols.

options.text: Alcohols have no hydrogen atoms at all
options.explanation: The OH group itself contains a hydrogen, and the chains carry many more.

questions.stem: State the functional group that every alcohol carries.
questions.modelAnswer: Every alcohol carries the hydroxyl group, written -OH.

questions.stem: State the type of solution formed when an alcohol mixes with water.
Explain why the -OH group is called the functional group of the alcohols.
questions.modelAnswer: Because the hydroxyl group is the part of the molecule responsible for the characteristic reactions of alcohols.

questions.stem: A colourless liquid mixes with water to give a neutral solution and burns as a fuel. Name the family it belongs to and state the functional group that decides this.
questions.modelAnswer: It is an alcohol: it carries the hydroxyl group, -OH, the functional group responsible for the characteristic reactions of the family.

options.text: C2H5OH
options.explanation: The two-carbon alcohol carries five chain hydrogens plus the hydroxyl hydrogen.

options.text: CH3OH
options.explanation: That is methanol, the one-carbon member of the family.

options.text: C2H5COOH
options.explanation: That formula belongs to the acid family, not the alcohols.

options.text: C3H7OH
options.explanation: Three carbons is propan-1-ol, one rung above ethanol.

questions.stem: How is the name of an alcohol built from the alkane name?

options.text: The final e of the alkane name is replaced with ol
options.explanation: Methane to methanol, ethane to ethanol: one letter swap records the OH group.

options.text: The stem is replaced with the word alcohol
options.explanation: The stem stays; only the ending changes.

options.text: The suffix ane is replaced with ene
options.explanation: That is the alkene rule; alcohols take the ol ending.

options.text: A prefix hydro- is added to the alkane name
options.explanation: No hydro- prefix exists in this system.

questions.stem: What does the 1 in propan-1-ol record?

options.text: That the OH group sits on the first carbon atom
options.explanation: The number is the address of the hydroxyl group along the three-carbon chain.

options.text: That the molecule contains one carbon
options.explanation: The stem prop already fixes three carbons; the 1 locates the group.

options.text: That the alcohol is the first member of the family
options.explanation: Methanol is the first member; the number is about position, not order.

options.text: That one water molecule is attached
options.explanation: The OH is bonded into the molecule, not water stuck on.

questions.stem: Which name is acceptable in the exam for propan-1-ol?

options.text: Propanol
options.explanation: The exam hint states the names propanol and butanol are acceptable.

options.text: Propane
options.explanation: That is the alkane with no OH group at all.

options.text: Propyl
options.explanation: Propyl is a fragment name, not the compound name.

options.text: Propanone
options.explanation: That belongs to the ketone family beyond this course.

questions.stem: Which displayed formula correctly shows butan-1-ol?

options.text: A four-carbon chain with the OH group bonded to the end carbon
options.explanation: Butan-1-ol places the hydroxyl on carbon one of the four-carbon chain, as the table shows.

options.text: A three-carbon chain with OH in the middle
options.explanation: Both the chain length and the group position are wrong for butan-1-ol.

options.text: A four-carbon chain with a C=C double bond
options.explanation: A double bond would make it an alkene; alcohol chains are single-bonded.

options.text: A four-carbon chain with OH on every carbon
options.explanation: One hydroxyl group per molecule is the rule at this level.

questions.stem: State the molecular formula of methanol.
State the acceptable shortened name for propan-1-ol in exams.
questions.modelAnswer: Propanol is the acceptable shortened name.

questions.stem: Explain what the 1 in propan-1-ol records about the molecule.
questions.modelAnswer: It records that the -OH group sits on the first carbon atom of the carbon chain.

questions.stem: An alcohol has three carbon atoms in its chain and the -OH group on the first carbon. State its full name.
